item.content:encoded:
A skeletal frame of reclaimed timber surrounds the elongated form of Skroget, a community sauna and public deck in Norway designed by student architecture studio Rare Collectiv.

Overlooking the busy harbour of Båtsfjord, known as Norway's fishing capital, the structure was designed and built by 15 students from the Design in Context course at the Norwegian University of Science and Technology (NTNU).

Named Skroget after the Norwegian word for hull, the 40-metre-long structure is modelled on the skeletal frame of a boat. It contains public seating areas, a sauna room and a terrace with a fire pit overlooking a rocky bank at the water's edge.

The design was developed collaboratively by the Rare Collectiv team, beginning with 15 individual proposals that were then discussed, developed and narrowed down to three designs, before a final vote.

"For us, the line where the sea meets the land was the most interesting part of the site, and we wanted to be able to connect the sauna experience close to the cold water so in future it is possible to create a bathing possibility," Rare Collectiv told Dezeen.

"Through the long building we created two sides – a rough waterside and a more protected side toward the land and south. Even with stronger winds, the walls provide shelter to enjoy the sun from the south," it added.

"Together, the wooden frames evoke the carcass of a fish, or, as suggested by the name of the project, the hull of a ship."

Almost the entire structure of Skroget was built with lengths of reused timber, sourced from a building recently dismantled by the local municipality.

Its defining feature is the row of nineteen timber portals, which have been angled towards the harbour to create a sloping roof that extends to shelter a walkway and seating area on the southern side.

Read:

Rezen transforms hotel stables in Australia into "raw and direct" wellness centre

This walkway links the more public entrance and fire pit to the west to the sauna at the eastern end, with the space in between housing changing rooms and showers.

"This concept of the continuous hallway allows visitors to explore the building without a dead end, but rather exit and explore a different space of the site," the team explained.

Contrasting with the predominantly reclaimed-wood structure, the 15-square-metre sauna was constructed from new wooden elements, with a dark brown wooden exterior and a pale birch interior.

For Skroget's external furniture, the team created a family of benches, tables and chairs with sloping seats and backrests designed to echo the building's angular frames.

Elsewhere in Norway, Rabagast Studio – led by students from the Norwegian University of Science and Technology in Trondheim – created a small timber sauna floating atop a lake in Innlandet.

Other saunas recently featured on Dezeen include a crystal-shaped structure in northern Sweden by Bigert & Bergström and Puusauna in Finland, which Jaakko Torvinen supported with a colonnade of tree trunks.

The photography is by Merethe Amundsen Ruud unless otherwise stated.

item.content:encoded:
A monolithic grey-brick home in Northern Ireland and a skinny house in Kyoto are among the most popular houses featured on Dezeen this month.

Also included in our monthly roundup of our readers' favourite residences is a lime-rendered house in Mexico, a cross-laminated timber holiday home in Sweden and a home in India built alongside mango trees.

Read on to find out more about Dezeen readers' favourite houses this month:

House and Studio in Kyoto, Japan, by Tato Architects

Measuring four by 30 metres, local studio Tato Architects filled this narrow site in Kyoto with a skinny home and ceramics studio illuminated by two skylit voids.

Inside, zigzagging staircases and walkways connect the home's separate eastern and western wings, which are elevated over an expansive ground-floor studio.

Find out more about House and Studio in Kyoto ›

Tollymore, UK, by McGonigle McGrath

Belfast studio McGonigle McGrath set six staggered rectangular volumes into a steep bank to form this riverside house in Northern Ireland.

Grey brick walls were built atop a stepped plinth formed from board-marked concrete, while large windows and glass doors overlook the surrounding nature.

Find out more about Tollymore ›

Casa Amona, Mexico, by Colar

Perched beside a wooded hill in San Cristóbal de las Casas, Casa Amona is a two-storey home and studio wrapped in white lime-rendered walls.

The home was designed by local architecture studio Colar for a multi-generational family, with a stacked layout of rooms that function as independent units and an enclosed ground-floor living space that can convert into a bedroom without architectural intervention.

Find out more about Casa Amona ›

Pine House, Sweden, by Johan Sundberg Arkitektur

Pine House stretches across a forested landscape in southern Sweden with a low-lying cross-laminated timber structure arranged in a cross-shaped plan.

Swedish studio Johan Sundberg Arkitektur wrapped the three-bedroom holiday home with pine panelling that was left exposed and untreated to weather over time.

Find out more about Pine House ›

House Beyond the Mango Trees, India, by InLe Architect

Indian practice InLe Architects shaded the interiors of this home in Kerala with timber shutters and the cooling canopy of two large mango trees.

The entrance is positioned between the trees, which leads to an elongated dining room designed as the heart of the home, and an adjacent outdoor patio.

Find out more about House Beyond the Mango Trees ›

item.content:encoded:
British carmaker Vauxhall has updated its griffin emblem, which has been pared back and lost its flag for the first time.

The logo is the 13th iteration of the brand's logo, which has incorporated a griffin since 1915.

In the latest update, Vauxhall's previous flat logo introduced in 2020 was further simplified, with the griffin made more angular. In particular, the mythical creature's neck hair was simplified while its beak was closed.

For the first time in the logo's 121-year history, the flag depicting the letter V no longer forms part of the logo.

"The griffin emblem is instantly recognisable, with Vauxhalls seen on almost every street in Britain," said Vauxhall design vice-president Mark Adams.

"Having adorned our vehicles in different forms for more than 120 years, we wanted to retain its essential elements while streamlining it for the next generation of electrified vehicles."

The revamped logo will be presented next month at the Paris Motor Show on the Vauxhall STX Concept. It will then be used on all future production models.

According to Vauxhall, the simplified logo was designed to be illuminated on its future electric vehicles.

Read:

Bentley unveils "biggest change" to logo in 100-year history

"As the griffin is now illuminated on the front of our latest models, this simpler design also makes it clearer and easier to identify," said Adams.

"The new look is sharper, cleaner and fits perfectly with the next evolution of our bold and pure design language."

The original griffin logo, designed by an apprentice at the company Harry Varley, was the winner of a competition to create a badge for the emerging car brand in 1915.

Varley incorporated the mythical creature into the logo as a nod to the coat of arms of Sir Falkes de Bréauté, who in the 13th century became the owner of the land in London now known as Vauxhall. This is where the car company, which began as the Vauxhall Ironworks, was first established.

Other car companies that have recently updated their logos include Bentley, which revealed the "biggest change" to its logo in its 100-year history last year.

All imagery courtesy of Vauxhall.

item.content:encoded:
The Royal Institute of British Architects has paid £150,000 to its former president Alan Jones, settling a long-running legal dispute over its handling of his personal information.

The £150,000 payment was listed in a draft of the institute's annual financial report, seen by the British magazine Architect's Journal (AJ), which broke the news yesterday.

In the draft, the payment is listed as a "settlement agreement" to an "ex-officio trustee". The AJ ascertained that this was Jones.

Payment followed long-term legal dispute

The payment concluded a long-term legal dispute between Jones and the Royal Institute of British Architects (RIBA), which was settled in 2025. It was sparked by the organisation's handling of personal information and allegations about Jones, which were leaked to the press in 2020.

RIBA has since stated that the organisation is "bound by its confidentiality obligations, which prevent further comment", AJ reported. However, it remains uncontested that the money was sent to Jones.

Read:

RIBA president Chris Williamson to give up architect title

Jones is a Northern Ireland-based architect and academic who became RIBA president in September 2019.

In early 2020, RIBA submitted a "serious incident report" involving Jones to the organisation's regulator, the Charity Commission, and the architect temporarily stepped down from his role as president. Details of this report were subsequently leaked to the media.

Jones returned to his role in June 2020 following an independent investigation by law firm Browne Jacobson, which cleared him to return to office.

Dispute caused by "unauthorised" disclosure of information

When the dispute was settled in 2025, RIBA said it regretted the "unauthorised" divulgence of information about its president.

"RIBA has reached a confidential settlement with the past president of RIBA, professor Alan Jones, in respect of his claim that information relating to him was not adequately protected and controlled by RIBA," RIBA chair Jack Pringle said at the time.

"RIBA regrets the fact that unauthorised leaks occurred and the harm that this caused professor Jones and his family."

Jones was succeeded as president of RIBA by Simon Allford in 2021. Allford was followed by Muyiwa Oki, and later today's president Chris Williamson.

Williamson, who is co-founder of Weston Williamson + Partners, recently caused a stir when giving up his architect title to draw attention to the "absurdity of the current regulatory framework" of ARB.

item.content:encoded:
A recyclable timber pavilion designed to mimic wildflowers is among the prototypes built by students at BuildFest 2026, shown in this video produced by Dezeen.

Designed by students from Lehigh University and Syracuse University, Wildflowers uses custom-designed 3D-printed joints to connect timber columns in an X shape that resembles flowers. It can be disassembled for future use.

BuildFest is a 3-day event held on the historic grounds of the 1969 Woodstock festival

The joints are fixed with simple hex bolts that leave three small holes in each piece so they can be removed and reused without damaging the timber.

The installation was part of BuildFest 2026, the fifth edition. The event returned to the historic grounds of the 1969 Woodstock festival in Bethel, New York and focused on large-scale structures designed to be adapted, dismantled and reused.

The festival marks the first instalment of a three-year curatorial initiative titled Acts of Construction.

Called Act One: Staging, the 2026 edition explored how the structures can accommodate different uses, performances and configurations, with future editions set to reuse and transform them.

At the edge of the forest, Proscenium by the University of Idaho used stump and roundwood rejected by commercial timber milling alongside dimensional lumber.

A timber truss framed a raised stage and suspended curtain, creating a performance space among the trees that recalled the Grand Stage at Woodstock.

Contact Hi-Fi by Cornell University was informed by prefabricated roof trusses and was constructed from pallet wood diverted from waste streams.

The installation featured modular trusses that can be rearranged into 12 configurations, with interchangeable panels featuring sonic transducers and sound-responsive lighting to create a backdrop for performances.

Also by Cornell University was BaleWorks, an installation and infrastructural prototype made from straw bales held within modular timber frames.

The structure doubles as a composting porta-john, bringing together agricultural waste, construction and public infrastructure.

At the festival's pond, the team from the University of California, Los Angeles constructed a floating modular ramp named Flotilla.

The raft could be assembled into a single structure, separated into individual rafts or rearranged to create spaces for performances.

Suspended among the trees, Flying Buttruss by Syracuse University & Rensselaer Polytechnic Institute was constructed using lumber, hardware and LED lights reused from last year's BuildFest.

The illuminated timber truss was relocated from the festival's camping ground to the forest, where it was raised between the trees and accompanied by a small bench made from leftover timber.

Read:

Students construct timber pavilions at Woodstock site during BuildFest

At night, several pavilions and installations were used for live performances and light shows.

BuildFest brings together students and faculty to design and build timber pavilions and multimedia installations as part of the Bethel Woods Art and Architecture Festival.

The 2026 festival took place over five days, with the installations remaining open to the public through November in Bethel, New York.

The photography is by Breyden Anderson and Kevin Furguson

BuildFest Acts of Construction took place from 9 to 13 September in Bethel, New York, with all installations remaining open until November. See Dezeen Events Guide for an up-to-date list of architecture and design events taking place around the world.

item.content:encoded:
Architecture studio Snøhetta added tunnelling playgrounds to Sky House, the final of four clubhouses that make up its Pavilia Farm residential development in Tai Wai, Hong Kong.

Called Sky House, the clubhouse was designed as a playground and fitness centre for all ages and combines play spaces with workout areas for senior residences.

It joins the Tea House, Well House and Farm House clubhouses, which opened in 2022 and were designed as a series of shared community spaces for a Hong Kong residential development centred around an urban farm.

An outdoor children's playground invites residents to the two-storey Sky House. Slides and platforms at various heights create an undulating landscape that extends into the interior ground floor, where a children's play area, a classroom and a music room are located.

Here, children can explore tunnels inside the hilly playground.

The upper floor comprises lounge spaces, fitness facilities and outdoor exercise areas designed for senior residents.

A domed skylight doubles as a rope-climbing tower at the centre of the building and connects the two floors, allowing natural daylight to fill the interiors.

"By bringing together spaces for different generations under one roof, Sky House supports meaningful encounters and strengthens community ties through everyday life," said Snøhetta.

Snøhetta intended for Pavilia Farm to introduce a new model of residential living – beyond offering private apartments in densely populated urban environments – that would support residents throughout all stages of their lives.

"Pavilia Farm began with a simple ambition: to create meaningful connections between residents, nature, and Hong Kong itself," said managing director of Snøhetta Asia Richard Wood.

"In one of the world's densest urban environments, the project provides a shared green sanctuary, the project demonstrates how architecture can shape relationships as much as it shapes space," he continued.

The studio has now completed all four clubhouses. These are arranged along a green farm at the centre of the development that offers residents access to shared gardens, urban farming and wellness facilities, as well as meeting and recreational spaces.

Each was designed to closely integrate with nature and respond to the surrounding mountains and the Shing Mun River.

The Tea House was designed as a cantilevered pavilion that overlooks the surrounding terraced landscape.

It has two water elements that were designed to have a calming effect – an outdoor pool on one side of the building and a cascading waterfall on the other.

Read:

Snøhetta unveils "green lung" urban farm in Hong Kong

The Well House, which is directly connected to the Tea House, has a gym, spa, sauna, an indoor pool and a badminton court.

Its galzed facade was designed to blur the boundary between architecture and landscape and bring people closer to nature.

At the heart of Pavilia Farm is the Farm House, which has three kitchens and a communal dining table to invite residents to cook and share meals together.

The clubhouse also features a bespoke table system that is supported by a moving rail on the floor and lets tables be combined or divided, depending on the size of the gathering.

According to Snøhetta, Pavilia Farm's layout was designed to encourage discovery and interaction.

"Rather than functioning as isolated amenities, the four clubhouses create a layered neighbourhood within the larger residential development, encouraging discovery, interaction, and participation in community life," said Snøhetta.

"Taken together, the four houses form more than a collection of communal facilities. They create a rich network of destinations woven into daily life, supporting residents of different ages, interests, and lifestyles."

Elsewhere, Snøhetta has recently completed Theodore Roosevelt Presidential Library in North Dakota, USA, as well as the extension of the Queensland Performing Arts Centre in Brisbane, Australia, wrapped in a rippling glass facade.

The photography is by Harold de Puymorin/HDP Photography.

item.content:encoded:
British architect Norman Foster is set to deliver a keynote speech at this year's Dezeen Awards party, which will take place at the Royal Opera House in London on 16 November.

In his address, Foster will focus on the future of architecture, drawing on his oeuvre as one of the most influential architects of his generation.

The nonagenarian is one of the world's most respected architects, leading global firm Foster + Partners alongside serving as president of the Norman Foster Foundation.

He has had an immense impact on global architecture over the past 60 years, with early landmark projects including the HSBC Building in Hong Kong and London Stansted Airport.

He remains at the helm of the global architectural powerhouse as executive chairman, with more recent significant projects including Apple Park in the USA and the Zayed National Museum in Abu Dhabi. The architect recently unveiled the final designs for memorial statues and a glass bridge dedicated to Queen Elizabeth II.

Foster is also one of the most decorated architects in history, being awarded the RIBA Gold Medal, AIA Gold Medal, Pritzker Architecture Prize and Praemium Imperiale award, while three buildings designed by his studio have won the Stirling Prize – including, most recently, a project described as the largest stone building built in the City of London since St Paul's Cathedral.

His foundation, along with his eponymous institute for sustainable cities launched in 2024, are initiatives that both promote interdisciplinary thinking and research to help new generations of architects, designers and urbanists anticipate the future as well as educating the civic leaders of the future.

Foster joined the architecture judging panel for Dezeen Awards 2026, alongside industry leaders Annabelle Selldorf, Daniel Libeskind, Ma Yansong and Amanda Levete, judging this year's projects which came from over 90 different countries across the globe.

Last week, Dezeen revealed all 392 shortlisted projects in the running for this year's awards. The architecture shortlist was announced on Monday, the interiors shortlist on Tuesday, followed by the design shortlist.

Read:

Ma Yansong and Daniel Libeskind join Dezeen Awards 2026 master jury in London

Readers can now choose their favourite shortlisted projects to be awarded in this year's public vote.

Amongst this year's shortlisted projects are a mosque with a perforated, blanket-like roof of stone-clad steelwork, an over-century-old dockside warehouse conversion and a modular furniture system made up of upholstered squishy balls.

Dezeen will announce the public vote winners and across social media channels ahead of the party on 16 November.

Tickets for the Dezeen Awards 2026 party are on sale. The occasion is an opportunity to celebrate with fellow nominees and VIPs, connect with others from around the world and reward your team for their hard work.

Studios that have been shortlisted for this year's Dezeen Awards are eligible to purchase discounted tickets for £249.

Subscribe to the Dezeen Awards newsletter to keep up to date with the latest announcements on the party.

Dezeen Awards is the ultimate accolade for architects and designers worldwide. The ninth edition of the annual awards is in partnership with global technology company Trimble. Through connected hardware and software solutions, Trimble helps designers to transform the way they shape spaces and buildings as well as drive productivity in the process. item.content:encoded:
Dezeen School Shows: a lamp crafted from volcanic stone and informed by a sunrise is among the projects from Instituto Tecnológico y de Estudios Superiores de Monterrey.

Also featured is a stone plate with a glass cloche referencing Mexican cinema, and a wooden stool featuring leather tassels.

Tecnológico de Monterrey

School: Architecture, Art and Design
Showcase: Inédito Universitario 2026 at Design Week México
Tutor: Luis Miguel Gutiérrez

School statement:

"In Mexico, black has been matter before pigment, an ancestral tradition in which colour is born from origin or from fire.

"Black takes up that heritage through contemporary design, with pieces whose tone comes from the material itself: black clay, volcanic stone, marble, charred wood and ceramics.

"As part of Design Week México, thirteen pieces, by design students at Tecnológico de Monterrey, were developed alongside artisans and workshops from different regions of Mexico.

"The exhibition core is monochromatic: every object is read through its form and the trace of the process that turned it black."

Estrato by Mariana Gayón García

"Estrato is a tabletop book organiser made of black volcanic stone that links the memory of the earth with the knowledge held in books.

"The design draws on the stone's natural qualities (weight, texture and density), turning them into part of its function of holding and organising books.

"The piece comes from understanding matter as memory. Volcanic stone carries the history of the land, and its black colour evokes the wisdom and knowledge inherited from earlier generations.

"That material memory meets the intellectual memory held in books, bringing materiality, memory and knowledge together in a functional, contemporary object."

Student: Mariana Gayón García
Course: Black: A Study of Mexican Dark Matter

Tatemada by Gabriela Covarrubias Rodríguez

"Tatemada is a table lamp made of black clay from Oaxaca that brings artisanal pottery together with contemporary design, turning a traditional material into a decorative lighting object for interior spaces.

"Inspired by Oaxaca's traditional smoke kitchens, the piece reinterprets the trace that fire and the passage of time leave on objects and the spaces they inhabit.

"Its rough finish evokes the soot that builds up on surfaces, while the warm light emerging from its openings stands for the warmth of a wood fire."

Student: Gabriela Covarrubias Rodríguez
Course: Black: A Study of Mexican Dark Matter
Tutor: Luis Miguel Gutiérrez

Comitl by Lucía Gallegos Bátiz

"Comitl is a decorative vessel inspired by the shape and structure of the cuexcomate, the ancestral structure used to store corn.

"Its silhouette draws on the essence of these ancient corn containers and reinterprets it for the present day. The rounded body extends into a conical section, creating a contrast between textures and elements.

"The piece seeks to recover and reinterpret the design, knowledge and forms of ancient Mexico from a contemporary point of view."

Student: Lucía Gallegos Bátiz
Course: Black: A Study of Mexican Dark Matter
Tutor: Luis Miguel Gutiérrez

Inframundo by Juan Pablo Castillo Villalón

"Inframundo starts from the colour black, understood not as a finish, but as the natural outcome of a material process.

"In the Mesoamerican worldview, black was linked to the underworld: a sacred space of transition where darkness did not signal an end, but the origin of transformation, life and rebirth.

"Working from that idea, the piece is a ceramic set made up of a cup and a filter for preparing cacao. Joined together, the two pieces evoke the silhouette of a pre-Hispanic vessel, and their geometry – divided into three sections – represents the underworld, the world of humans and the celestial world.

"The black colour emerges naturally during firing through glazes with natural pigments and reduction reactions, making the transformation of the ceramic visible.

"More than a utensil, the piece proposes a contemporary ritual for preparing cacao, inviting people to rediscover this ingredient with respect for its origin."

Student: Juan Pablo Castillo Villalón
Course: Black: A Study of Mexican Dark Matter
Tutor: Luis Miguel Gutiérrez

Veda by Emanuel Reyes Díaz

"Veda is an appetiser plate that uses a frosted glass dome to progressively cover and reveal the food arranged on a volcanic stone base.

"The piece takes as its reference the way censorship in Mexican cabaret cinema (cine de ficheras) concealed certain images, leaving room for fantasy and desire.

"The device is carried over into the act of eating, drawing a parallel between desire and appetite through anticipation, reveal and enjoyment."

Student: Emanuel Reyes Díaz
Course: Black: A Study of Mexican Dark Matter
Tutor: Luis Miguel Gutiérrez

Bartola by Alejandra Arnaud Escobar

"Bartola is a stool inspired by cowboy aesthetics and guided by the Japanese philosophy of conscious use of resources, built in purpleheart wood, leather and brass fittings.

"The piece revalues traditional crafts – carpentry, leatherwork and jewellery-making – bringing them together in a contemporary object that puts materiality, craft and permanence first.

"According to its own author, Bartola rests on three core ideas: craft, because it seeks to revalue traditional techniques; material, because the materials are the protagonists of the design; and character, because every detail is meant to communicate identity and permanence.

"The piece aims to become a statement object, capable of showing that furniture can preserve crafts, reinterpret traditions and create meaningful experiences."

Student: Alejandra Arnaud Escobar
Course: Black: A Study of Mexican Dark Matter
Tutor: Luis Miguel Gutiérrez

Bucle by Paulina Ibarra Gutiérrez

"Bucle is a modular shelving system built around a crocheted wire panel, scaling jewellery-making processes up into functional, contemporary furniture.

"The piece does not treat manual work as a disadvantage against industry, but instead challenges its historical devaluation as domestic labour.

"By bringing it into contemporary design with a high level of technical rigour, it becomes a statement of exclusivity, intentionality and precision."

Student: Paulina Ibarra Gutiérrez
Course: Black: A Study of Mexican Dark Matter
Tutor: Luis Miguel Gutiérrez

Rastro by Tamara Cagigal Esclusa

"Rastro is a modular system made of two charred-wood pieces that, combined, generate different patterns and compositions for cladding or decorating walls.

"Its reliefs evoke the textures of cooling lava, and the contrast between geometry, texture and materiality turns each composition into a surface that transforms the space.

"The piece grows out of the idea that transformation does not disappear, but remains as a trace. It interprets the solidification of lava through charred wood, carrying the memory of a process of change into a new material."

Student: Tamara Cagigal Esclusa
Course: Black: A Study of Mexican Dark Matter
Tutor: Luis Miguel Gutiérrez

El Resguardo – Teresa, Carola and Lidia by Anabella Cariño Olivier

"El Resguardo is a family of three containers – Teresa, Carola and Lidia – made of black Tecali marble with charred maple lids.

"The collection combines the weight, shine and permanence of stone with the warmth of a wood transformed by fire, in soft, compact forms meant for keeping personal, everyday objects.

"The project starts from the act of keeping close what we choose to hold on to. It explores the contrast between two dark materials: marble, mineral and polished, which reflects light; and charred maple, organic and transformed by fire, which absorbs it.

"The natural variations in grain and tone of each block of marble are kept as evidence of the material's origin and of each piece's craft process."

Student: Anabella Cariño Olivier
Course: Black: A Study of Mexican Dark Matter
Tutor: Luis Miguel Gutiérrez

Tlecuil by Sophie Nicole Aguilar Ramírez

"Tlecuil is a table lamp that holds a sunrise. A crater carved into a volcanic stone base is where the light lives.

"The bulb barely peeks out from its upper half, like a sun rising between mountains, and a hand-dyed cotton cloth shade fades from black to ochre, letting that first glow escape.

"The name comes from the Nahuatl word for hearth, the hollow where fire is kept. The piece draws on the Legend of the Suns, in which Nanahuatzin throws himself into the hearth, and his sacrifice lights the fifth sun.

"With that, it proposes black not as absence or death, but as the origin from which all light is born. Darkness is the condition for fire to exist, and fire the condition for light to exist."

Student: Sophie Nicole Aguilar Ramírez
Course: Black: A Study of Mexican Dark Matter
Tutor: Luis Miguel Gutiérrez

item.content:encoded:
North American football league Major League Soccer has moved its New York headquarters to the Penn 2 skyscraper and commissioned US studio TPG Architecture to have it mirror the dynamics of a soccer pitch.

The office opened earlier this year just before the 2026 FIFA World Cup, which also coincided with the thirtieth anniversary of the Major League Soccer (MLS) organisation and football's "surging cultural momentum", according to TPG Architecture.

The two-storey office integrates elements from a football stadium, according to the studio, such as an entrance area that resembles the tunnel players run through to enter the field.

"The 'office as a stadium' concept emerged from feedback the MLS Commissioner had collected from current and former players, coaches, retired athletes, and long-standing employees about what they hoped to see in the new headquarters," said the studio.

"The architectural layout mirrors the dynamics of a soccer pitch, utilising fluid curves inspired by the physics of a moving ball and the momentum of the game to inform how the space is experienced."

Visitors enter through the tunnelled elevator bay clad in custom mesh weave that is "goalie net-esque". LED lighting behind the walls and ceiling-mounted LED screens can be programmed to display branding for visitors, clubs, or sponsors, according to the studio.

This space leads into a reception area, and beyond that, a double-height lobby is centred around a grand staircase. A wall of jerseys surrounds one side of the reception area, while the Championship Cup is displayed on a pedestal on the other.

The grand staircase connects to spaces such as meditation and wellness rooms, coffee bars and a bottom-floor cafe that are together referred to as the Midfield, or a central space where employees can gather and interact.

The staircase itself is lined with a digital LED banner that represents different tiers of a stadium, and flashes players and branding.

At the bottom level, the floors open up into the cafe area and a "dugout-style" IT technical corner that takes cues from the technical area of a stadium, where coaches gather during a game.

Read:

HOK unveils Major League Soccer's first fully electric stadium in Queens

Elsewhere, conference and meeting rooms are lined with screens and primarily grey carpeting and seating. Bold "grass green" and cobalt "MLS-blue" tones were also used across furniture and accents.

Employee working floors are lined with a patterned carpet and desk units.

The studio said it incorporated a diagonal slash motif throughout the project, pulling from the MLS shield logo, which features an elongated slash across its centre.

TPG Architecture also completed a headquarters for the NHL in Manhattan and the office of an advertising agency in North Carolina.

The MLS is the primary football league in the United States and Canada and was founded in 1996 after the US hosted the 1994 World Cup.

Dezeen recently rounded up the 23 stadiums slated to host the 2030 World Cup.

item.description:

item.content:encoded:
With AI driving demand, vast data centres are increasingly in the news as people question the impact on local environments. Can architects help to make these buildings look and function better?

When was the last time that buildings animated the population of the United States as much as the current wave of data centre development?

In the past two years, the huge, boxy buildings have provoked backlash across partisan lines as plans have been announced across suburban and rural America.

Housing the servers that power cloud computing and, now, artificial intelligence (AI), data centres are an important part of the infrastructure that supports the internet.

Usually located in sparsely populated areas, these nondescript buildings have been largely ignored as architecture, but this is beginning to change.

"Data centers are, in general, an example of poor design," Spanish academic Marina Otero Verzier, who won the 2022 Wheelwright Prize for her theories on data centres, told Dezeen.

With growing public awareness of data centres' heavy land, water and energy use, pushback has been intense. Nearly 70 per cent of the US population opposes their construction. Yet the US is set to double its data centre building to keep pace with the boom in AI, with spending on data centre infrastructure projected to top $800 billion per year globally in 2026.

Architects are largely absent from the trend – something that Otero Verzier believes needs to change if there is any hope of these structures being positive, or at least neutral, contributors to the built environment.

"Architects should be involved in the design of the building – from the materials used to the metabolic relations it establishes with the environment and communities – as well as in thinking about their public nature as repositories of collective knowledge and their broader urban and territorial planning," she said.

"Architects have a ton of value to add to the data center conversation"

So far, that hasn't happened, and even some developers recognise data centres have suffered from a lack of design thinking.

Daniel English, co-founder and managing partner of Legacy Investing, a real estate firm that specialises in data centres, believes that architects were sidelined in the early designs of data centres, because the buildings were treated as engineering projects.

Read:

Study links data centres to heat island effects worldwide

"Architects have a ton of value to add to the data center conversation, and I think that they got left out because it was possible to build buildings just based on efficiency," he said. "Data centres are so new that we're still figuring out what they look like."

However, he believes that now is the time to be giving more thought to how they look.

With construction already a huge source of carbon emissions, it may be that the best design when it comes to data centres is not building at all. But right now the market is saying build.

"It's not like we're not going to have data centers," said English. "The conversation today should be how to make sure that these are thoughtfully integrated into our lives."

"The architecture of the building does matter"

Until the AI bubble pops – as investors have warned – or an unlikely national referendum on the buildings happens, they look set up to keep going. So what role should architects play?

At present, architect involvement in data centre design often comes from corporate firms large enough to have a full data centre division. Gensler is one of the design-forward firms that is competing for data centre commissions.

It is currently designing a 7.5 GW hyperscale data centre in Utah for O'Leary Digital, and a cluster of five data centres for Menlo Digital in Arizona. At both sites, renders show facade treatments designed to improve the appearance of the buildings – striated facades to match the desert mountains in Utah and Corten steel in Arizona.

This move towards beautification or – in some cases, camouflage – represents one of the main ways architects are having an impact on these buildings.

"I think with good design, with proper architectural gestures, you can either make these buildings blend in or stand out, and I think that it's going to come up more and more as these buildings need to become a little bit more local," Gensler critical facilities practice leader Rob LoBuono told Dezeen.

"The architecture of the building does matter," continued LoBuono. "We really do find that a well-designed building has a strong impact in the community, even if the current opinion of them is, you know, fluid."

Otero Verzier, for her part, doesn't believe that the role of the architect should be reduced to facades.

"The idea that the most architects can do is design a facade is quite sad and says more about the lack of ambition of the profession than about the reality of data centres," said Otero Verzier.

"If, as a profession," she added, "we want to be completely irrelevant, then we can focus on designing facades for data centres."

Integrating data centres into urban schemes

During the 2025 Venice Architecture Biennale, architecture studio Grimshaw presented an integrated urban plan based around data centre development, bringing the typology firmly into conversations around speculative architecture.

Informed by a real project with developer Goodman, the proposal positions the data centre development as "the catalyst of a mixed-use renewal precinct – next to homes, studios, shops and even an urban farm". The proposal would pump the data centre's waste heat back into the surrounding buildings.

"Close quarters aren't a liability; they're the key that lets resources circulate instead of being wasted," said Grimshaw in the brief.

Legacy Investing's English told Dezeen that it was already developing several data centres integrated into wider mixed-use schemes, while the architecture studios we spoke to were broadly positive about the concept.

Unsurprisingly, the biggest data centre developers don't seem to be paying much attention to the thinking coming out of architecture biennales.

Efficiencies and monumental boxes are, and will probably remain, the norm.

Corgan director of data centres Tom Kruger, said that integrating data centres within other structures and wider developments is an "exception and not the rule". He explained that concerns over security and power mean that remote locations are preferred.

"A big part of that is aiming for security and sound isolation," he told Dezeen.

Read:

Gensler designs Corten data centre to have "meaningful civic contribution"

A more realistic vision for mixed-use data centres probably looks closer to a contemporary tech campus than the Grimshaw model. Most of the architects Dezeen spoke with mentioned landscaping or parklands around the data centres, though they noted these plans run up against security concerns.

Both largely sterile and industrial in size, data centres represent a unique sort of infrastructure.

Rather than likening these buildings to warehouses or power plants, English compared data centres to parking infrastructure. He believes that they can be integrated into buildings or placed underground, and not just housed in standalone buildings.

"Parking to me is an interesting analogy because parking can be an entire building; it can be part of a building," said English. "In that way, compute can be part of a building; it can be a whole building."

Of course, parking lots have more often than not been blights on the urban and suburban landscape.

Elevated data centres

Recent projects, such as an SOM data centre skyscraper in Kansas City, show that some developers are pushing beyond the typical horizontal spread, especially where, like in this case, rural zoning laws have made developing sprawling hyperscale centres difficult.

However, architects Dezeen spoke to said building tall makes little sense, with the high price tags and sensitivity of the servers, the need for easy maintenance and the speed of building.

Most large data centres are built in areas outside of cities, with plenty of land – and land usage is a large part of the public's complaint.

Kruger, who has worked in the field for 16 years, said that he does see these centres becoming more "elevated" from an architectural perspective, though mainly through technologies that make them more energy efficient.

Other companies have proposed using older structures, as with Terawulf's plans to build a data centre in a decommissioned Kentucky smelter.

Microsoft has built data centres using mass timber in a show of healthier building materials. Meanwhile, their energy demands have revived talks of nuclear energy integration in the United States.

"Repositories of collective knowledge"

Otero Verzier envisions a more distributed future in which data centres are not commercial concentrations but public "repositories" of knowledge.

"As long as data centres start being designed with attention to the diverse ecologies of data – cold, hot, long-lasting, and temporary, open, public or private – to the limits and rhythms of the planet and its inhabitants, we can begin to develop more relevant architectures that do not necessarily look like closed-off boxes or bunkers, but instead take the form of public institutions.

If architecture can help reimagine the way these buildings look and function, through the largesse of developers concerned about buildings – or just concerned about their reception – perhaps the way they're used can change too.

item.content:encoded:
Dezeen Showroom: local production, repairability and honest design are foregrounded in Norwegian brand Hegren's Knekt floor lamp.

Designed for the contemporary home, where people might use an armchair to work in as much as relax in, the Knekt lamp provides directional light that is easily angled and height-adjusted.

Like all of Hegren's products, it is designed with a focus on repairability and longevity, using standard components as much as possible so they can be replaced if needed.

Its form is intended to be pure and easy to understand, with a lampshade bent from a single laser-cut sheet of locally sourced aluminium and an aluminium arm and body.

"As a designer, I work within clear constraints – letting material, production and function shape the design from the beginning," said Hegren founder Henrik Grevstad.

"With Knekt, the open construction is both a functional consideration and an important part of the design. The structure is kept visible rather than hidden, giving the lamp a clear and honest character while remaining visually light."

Among Knekt's other practical features are an E27 socket for straightforward bulb replacement, an off-switch integrated into the lamp head for easy access, and flat-packed shipping with no-tool assembly.

item.content:encoded:
Architecture studio Stanton Williams has completed two boarding houses for girls at Winchester College, wrapping courtyards with gabled brick buildings that reference the historic layout and architecture of the 640-year-old site.

Winchester College was originally founded in 1382, and the project is its first new boarding complex since 1912. It is also the first in its history designed for girls since the school moved to co-education in 2022.

Stanton Williams aimed to ground the scheme in both the site's historic architecture and the "culture of the college", using familiar materials and a layout based on its historic buildings and cloisters.

"We started by trying to understand Winchester on its own terms – not just its buildings, but how the college works and how pupils learn and live together," the studio's principal director Kaori Ohsugi told Dezeen.

"Because these houses are for sixth formers, we were also interested in the space between a school and a college – somewhere that provides comfort and security, but also encourages independence, conversation and the exchange of ideas," she added.

"That thinking shaped the courtyards, cloister and sequence of shared spaces, so the architecture supports the culture of the college rather than simply providing accommodation."

The two boarding houses form an S-shape that encloses two courtyard gardens on either side, with rows of gable roofs helping break down the massing of the blocks.

Overlooking the central courtyards are two back-to-back dining halls with fully glazed walls and skylit timber ceilings, which can be united as a single large space via a movable partition wall.

"Each house has its own dining hall – its own heart, in a sense – but the wall can open and the two courts, the two communities, come together," Ohsugi explained.

"It's a small architectural move, but it carries the whole idea of the project, two houses that are distinct but never separate," she added.

Read:

David Kohn Architects curves University of Oxford college building around three-sided quadrangles

Alongside the dining areas, the ground floor of the blocks accommodates communal and staff spaces, while above, two floors of bedrooms are organised off central corridors to either overlook the courtyard or the surrounding campus.

Brickwork on the exterior of the blocks references the college's Victorian boarding houses, with varying bonds, textured areas and patches of flint incorporated into the garden walls.

Inside, this is complemented by warm oak panelling incorporating perforated acoustic panels. This matches the glue-laminated timber beams of the dining halls.

"Brick was never in question – it's what the Victorian boarding houses are built from, supplied here by brick manufacturer York Handmade as a blend of four colours," explained Ohsugi.

"We varied the bonds according to how each part of the building is used," added Ohsugi. "Flemish bond at ground level, where people experience the wall at close range, references Antrim House and the historic core."

"A vertical stretcher bond marks the transition at the cloister openings, and 'hit-and-miss' brickwork sits in front of the staircase windows, giving soft, dappled light and a degree of privacy without feeling closed off," she added.

Stanton Williams is a Stirling Prize-winning London architecture studio founded by Alan Stanton and Paul Williams in 1985.

Its previous projects include a retirement complex overlooking Hampstead Heath in London and the renovation and extension of the Grade II*-listed Rhodes House at the University of Oxford.

The studio won the Stirling Prize in 2012 for the Sainsbury Laboratory in the botanic gardens of Cambridge University.

item.content:encoded:
Architecture studio Populous has unveiled its design for the Rach Chiec Stadium in Ho Chi Minh City, which will become the country's national stadium.

Set to be built on the outskirts of the city, the stadium will be the largest in the country when completed, with around 30,000 seats more than the current record holder – the Mỹ Đình National Stadium.

The stadium will be wrapped in a diamond-patterned facade that, according to the studio, was informed by the shape of Nipa Palms that grow alongside rivers in the area.

It will be covered by a fully retractable roof that will allow the playing area to be environmentally controlled, while also shielding the surrounding residential areas from noise.

Rach Chiec Stadium is designed to host team sports such as football, but also "90 per cent of Olympic sports". It forms part of a wider plan to improve the country's sporting facilities with the aim of hosting major events including the Southeast Asian Games, Asian Cup and potentially a future Olympics.

The stadium will be built as part of a 200-hectare Rach Chiec National Sports Complex, masterplanned by Populous, which will also include an 18,000-seat arena.

Read:

Populous completes Buffalo Bills stadium in New York

"The stadium and arena design are informed by the masterplan for the entire precinct, providing anchors for a park-like experience, supported by commercial offerings and activations," said Populous senior principal Andrew Tulen.

"We are focusing on making the venues accessible, well connected and flexible to provide a variety of experiences for all demographics."

One of the world's most prolific stadium designers, Populous is currently designing stadiums for the Tampa Bay Rays professional baseball team in the USA and a stand for Wrexham AFC in the UK.

It is also currently renovating the "home of Indian cricket" in Kolkata, Estádio da Luz stadium in Lisbon for Benfica and the King Fahd Sports City Stadium in Riyadh.

item.content:encoded:
One of the oldest surviving pharmacies in the world, Florence's Officina Profumo-Farmaceutica di Santa Maria Novella, has appointed Italian design duo Formafantasma as creative directors.

Their new role will see studio founders Andrea Trimarchi and Simone Farresin focus primarily on the company's products.

The studio aims to unravel their hidden histories and inform new launches, while also sharing input across Officina Profumo-Farmaceutica di Santa Maria Novella's packaging, communication, retail spaces and events.

"Our intention is not to redefine Santa Maria Novella through a new image, but to build from what already exists, understanding what has allowed it to remain relevant since 1221 and how this can inform its present and future," Formafantasma said.

"This means examining how its history is communicated, how new products are developed, and how the different expressions of the company can form a coherent whole."

The Officina was founded in 1221 by Dominican friars, who grew medicinal herbs and used them to prepare remedies, balms and ointments for the infirmary of Florence's Santa Maria inter Vineas church.

Over the centuries, it became a public pharmacy, official supplier to the Medici court and later a purveyor of cosmetics and fine fragrances, making it one of the oldest continuously operating pharmacies in the world. Today, it functions largely as a perfumery.

"The Officina is not simply defined by its longevity, but by the accumulation and transmission of knowledge across generations, embedded in ingredients, formulations, techniques, objects and spaces," Formafantasma said.

"Working with such an accumulation raises questions close to our own practice, particularly how it is preserved and transformed, how materials carry their own histories, and how an institution can advance without treating its past as static."

Read:

Formafantasma announced as ecology advisor to Serpentine Galleries

Material legacies are a well-trodden path for the design duo, known for its research-heavy deep dives into specific materials, whether charting the global impact of the forestry industry or unpacking wool production and our surprisingly symbiotic relationship with sheep.

For the Officina, the aim is for Formafantasma to apply this same forensic approach to materials and sustainability to the company's own uninterrupted production heritage in order to inform its future.

"Their role will be that of curators, attentive to the knowledge the Officina has safeguarded for eight centuries, made of ingredients, formulas and craft, and to the ways in which it can continue to evolve," the company said.

This isn't the first time that an institution has brought Formafantasma on board as an advisor in recent months. In July, the duo was also announced as the first-ever ecology advisor to London's Serpentine Galleries, where the designers previously hosted their Cambio exhibition.

Dezeen Showroom: designer Piergiorgio Cazzaniga and furniture brand Andreu World have added extra cushioning to one of their successful seating designs to make Capri Comfort – a minimalist executive chair that can now support longer periods of sitting.

Capri Comfort is an evolution of the Capri line of lounge and executive chairs, which have a light and pure expression defined by a slim upholstered back and seat and minimal visible mechanisms.

For Capri Comfort, Cazzaniga and Andreu World built out the seat and backrest with next-generation high-density foams, providing ergonomic support for modern executive offices, meeting rooms and home workspaces.

"Without altering the minimalist silhouette of the classic model, this design conveys a sense of understated luxury that invites long meetings or moments of reflection," said Andreu World.

The Capri Comfort chair is available with a choice of three backrest heights – low, medium or high – and three swivel bases, either with gliders or casters.

All versions include a tilting mechanism and pneumatic height adjustment to support dynamic sitting and enable a healthy recline, and come in a huge choice of fabrics including options from leading textile brands Kvadrat and Camira.

item.description:

item.content:encoded:
A former tile warehouse in Accra, Ghana, has been transformed into the headquarters of the African Futures Institute, an independent architecture school founded by Ghanaian-Scottish architect Lesley Lokko.

Designed by Lokko with designer Fred Swart and architects Patrick Gentilezza, Patti Anahory and Laurence Lord, the renovated building contains research and education spaces for the school and cultural spaces for the public to gather.

Situated in the neighbourhood of Osu, it is the first time the African Futures Institute has had a permanent home, after operating through partnerships and temporary spaces since its establishment in 2021.

"The refurbishment gives an existing commercial building in Osu a new civic life as a permanent centre for education, culture and public programming," African Futures Institute told Dezeen.

"Through lectures, exhibitions, workshops, screenings and gatherings, it creates a place where African Futures Institute's work can connect directly with the everyday life and rhythms of Accra," the institute continued.

"We hope people experience it as a framework for cultural activity rather than a conventional institutional building. Above all, it is intended to encourage learning, encounter and the exchange of ideas."

Read:

Lesley Lokko launches Nomadic African Studio as "a space to think about architecture differently"

Believed to have been constructed in the late 1950s or early 1960s, based on local oral history, the building envelope of the former tile warehouse was preserved and restored.

Skylights were added to the roof and new wall openings were designed to rationalise the facades.

Interior spaces were organised around the Urban Room, a multi-purpose flexible space that can operate as a lecture hall, studio, cinema, workshop and exhibition hall.

Rammed earth was used in the flooring and for a wall that extends the length of the building, which was finished with linseed oil.

Locally sourced clay bricks, quarry dust, hardwood, metalwork and precast concrete were used elsewhere in the building to form a material palette that complements the industrial former warehouse.

Last year, Lokko and the African Futures Institute launched the Nomadic African Studio educational program, which will continue operations in the new headquarters.

Lokko became the first African woman to win the RIBA Gold Medal in 2024 and was named on Time magazine's list of the 100 most influential people in the same year.

The photography is by Alix McIntosh.

item.content:encoded:
Anonymous London design duo City Girls creates one-off lighting out of reclaimed lace, coat hangers and scale models scavenged from eBay, Facebook Marketplace and the side of the road.

City Girls (stylised as city.girls.xp) is the studio and alias of two unnamed artists, who started making lamps together two years ago after bonding over a shared love of old knickknacks.

The north London duo are making a name for themselves by crafting one-of-a-kind pieces out of everything from discarded sequins to chains and feathers sourced second-hand on the internet or in real life, which at one point left them rooting through the debris of a smashed-up toy on the street.

Once each lamp is complete, it is affectionately named something like Pamela, Jean or Allegra, to give it a distinct identity.

Among the duo's growing collection is Zoe, a tall floor lamp characterised by a gridded metal frame wrapped in old jersey fabric, and embellished with goose feathers extracted from a hat.

Sabine, the pair's first working lamp, features a base crafted out of a fragment of an old chrome chair, topped with a translucent shade made of a fibreglass model boat.

Lola and Nina are a pair of boxy lamps cloaked with Glomesh sequins, a material that was also draped over the metallic Raquel.

City Girls has previously described the process of cobbling together its lighting as akin to the act of getting dressed, throwing together a mismatched outfit.

This visual style is especially clear in curving Virginia, made from old metal chair legs and crowned with a swan-like arched green head.

The duo also has a penchant for objects that show signs of fabrication through welds and seams, or anything else that nods to their former purpose.

City Girls named themselves after a Victorian novel by radical author Margaret Harkness called A City Girl, which details vivid descriptions of 1880s London streets.

Read:

Billy Easter's Gel Lamp shifts colour using transposable slides

The studio has been steadily growing its presence in the UK capital.

Over the summer, local interior designer Jermaine Gallacher curated the exhibition Ten Lamps by City Girls at the Ragged School, London Bridge.

During this month's London Design Festival, a wealth of other collectible design was on display in various city-wide exhibitions.

Among them was the second-ever Studio Iron show in South Kensington, curated by artist Isamaya Ffrench and featuring pieces by designers including Andu Masebo, Barnaby Lewis and Jane Wright.

The photography is courtesy of City Girls.

item.content:encoded:
Chinese studios HB Architects and Nature Times Art have completed a hotel in Jiashan, China, which is connected by a 360-metre-long raised walkway.

Named Dayun Landison Manor, the hotel occupies the elongated site of a demolished village. It stretches 360-metre-long from east to west, with a maximum width of 54 metres in the middle that narrows to 21 metres at the ends.

The hotel is formed of numerous buildings connected by a walkway raised 4.9 metres above ground. According to the studios, this horizontal layout is a nod to the history of the site and an attempt to recreate a village-like neighbourhood.

"We fictionalised a village to continue the functional essence of 'dwelling'," HB Architects and Nature Times Art told Dezeen.

The raised guest rooms were also designed to reference local housing, which is often supported on pilotis.

However, the columns supporting the structures were deliberately hidden to highlight the visual dominance of the horizontal slab that runs through the site.

The hotel's entrance opens into a courtyard with a lake at its centre and a "water curtain" that falls from surrounding walkway.

Guests then walk up stairs to the raised walkway that passes around courtyards and gardens to get to the rooms. A large pool occupies the tip at one end of the raised platform.

"The building offers more than just one kind of experience," said the studios. "You have to walk through it yourself to really get it."

Read:

Hotel Wuxi MGallery Collection informed by historical poet's home

While the rooms are arranged in blocks surrounding the raised walkway, more functional spaces were placed below the slab.

The upper blocks were painted earthy yellow, while the lower floor and walkways were painted terracotta red as a reference to the surrounding landscape.

"We deliberately chose to avoid white buildings," said HB Architects and Nature Times Art. "The colours we use in this building show how we think about nature."

"The main colours relate to our design keywords—'earth' or 'nature'," they continued.

HB Architects and Nature Times Art are architecture and interior practices based in Shenzhen.

Elsewhere in China, WATG and Wimberly Interiors have completed a boutique hotel in Wuxi's Dangkou Ancient Town, and BLUE Architecture Studio has transformed a cluster of new and old buildings in Yangzhou into a hotel complex.

The photography is by Guowei Liu.

item.content:encoded:
Promotion: the robust, precision-engineered quality of a restaurant kitchen can be recreated at home with Fisher & Paykel's latest Professional Style appliances.

The Professional Style appliances are one of three product design styles in the New Zealand brand's luxury range, alongside the Minimal and Contemporary offerings.

Fisher & Paykel aimed to bring the best qualities of professional cooking environments into the home, while offering the refinement and integration befitting a bespoke domestic kitchen.

High-grade stainless steel surfaces, easy-to-grab bull-nose handles and precise temperature and humidity controls characterise the products, which include ovens, hobs, refrigerators and wine cabinets.

Flush installation, smooth junctions and fine 2-millimetre gaps deliver on refinement, either imbuing products with an architectural presence of their own or concealing them seamlessly behind cabinetry.

"With the Professional Style, the intention is not for the appliance to disappear, but for it to feel completely resolved within the kitchen," said Fisher & Paykel head of industrial design (cooking) Adam Moody.

"The stainless-steel presence is deliberate, but so is the precision: the way the product aligns, the way it sits with surrounding cabinetry, and the way its proportions support the broader composition," he continued.

Fisher & Paykel identified the sights, sounds and rhythms of professional kitchens – "the movement of pans, the weight of metal in the hand, the choreography of preparation and service" – as part of their appeal and worked to translate those qualities into the design through robustness and tactility.

The design features precision-engineered dials on the cooktops and range cooker, and carefully calibrated oven doors and telescopic rails.

The Professional Style is part of Fisher & Paykel's vision to bring the "beauty of choice" to architects, designers and homeowners,
supporting the creation of bespoke kitchens with a cohesive aesthetic while delivering the same levels of performance.

The brand explained that this shift to seeing the kitchen as a social space with connected dining and living functions means appliances now need to be considered not only as tools, but also as design elements.

"Luxury is increasingly personal," said Fisher & Paykel. "Kitchens are no longer singular expressions of status or function, but more personal reflections of architecture, material preferences and ways of living."

"Fisher & Paykel's appliance design styles — Minimal, Contemporary and Professional— are crafted to support different forms of architectural expression."

In contrast to the Professional Style appliances, the Minimal and Contemporary Styles have a quieter visual presence, making use of smokey dark or lightly reflective silver-grey glass and slim or no handles.

Professional Style products come in a universal width of 76 centimetres for easy configuration.

Fisher & Paykel was founded in New Zealand in 1934. Find out more about the brand and its Professional Style luxury appliances on its website.

item.content:encoded:
US studio Coughlin Scheel Architects has completed the cedar-clad Surf Road House, lifting it 10 feet above the ground because of environmental concerns.

The house sits on Fire Island, a narrow barrier island in New York that is accessed by ferry. Motor vehicles are largely prohibited on the island, with its delicate landscape.

Situated outside the town of Ocean Beach, the house is located within a designated Coastal Erosion Hazard Area, which is an area with shorelines that are receding a foot or more per year, according to New York's Department of Environmental Conservation.

The property originally had a 1950s house, which was razed.

Due to federal, state and local rules, the design for the new home went through an "extended approvals process".

Ultimately, the pre-existing house enabled the team to "maximize the allowable footprint and add a second storey", said Brooklyn-based Coughlin Scheel Architects.

Due to flooding concerns, the house was lifted 10 feet (three metres) above the ground by wood pilings. The pilings go deep, stretching up to 35 feet (10.6 metres) below grade.

Rectangular in plan, it has a boxy form that is broken up with elements such as overhangs and pilasters that "introduce rhythm, depth and shadow".

The team incorporated both vertical and horizontal striped elements on the exterior, lending a linear quality to the building.

Facades are clad in cedar siding with a colouring that alludes to dunes and driftwood, helping the house feel connected to the landscape.

Large windows on the southern facade provide views of the ocean, while the home is more opaque on the north side, which overlooks a path.

A staircase and a switchback-style ramp – both enclosed within wood-slat walls – provide access to the main entrance, which is found on the first level.

"Since Fire Island is car-free, everyone brings items from the ferry in wagons – and every house needs a ramp," the team said.

"Ramps and stairs become an integral part of the design exercise and remain part of the Fire Island entry ritual."

Inside the 2,200-square-foot (204-square-metre) house, the first level contains an open-plan room for cooking, dining and lounging.

The communal area flows onto a terrace overlooking the beach. An outdoor shower enables occupants to wash off sand before heading indoors.

Read:

Six respectfully renovated modernist homes on Fire Island

The first floor also contains a bedroom suite, and three additional bedrooms are found on the top level.

The levels are connected by an interior staircase and an outdoor spiral staircase.

Interior features include white cabinetry, wooden wall cladding and slatted ceilings that draw upon the exterior aesthetic. A curved ceiling in the entryway "adds movement and softness to the more geometric, linear architectural gestures".

The space under the house, which is enclosed by wooden screens, contains beach gear and bikes.

Other Fire Island projects include a mid-century house that was renovated by the founders of BoND to be a "machine for voyeurism" and a cedar-clad 1960s house that was renovated and expanded by Andrew Franz.

The photography is by Alan Tansey.

item.content:encoded:
Architecture studio GRT Architects has modernised and updated New York architecture gallery Storefront for Art and Architecture, installing custom, removable shelving units and placing a doorknob on its facade for the first time.

The scope for the renovation included updating electrical and HVAC systems in the single, triangular gallery space at Storefront for Art and Architecture (Storefront) and adding flexible display units that can be adapted as needed for the gallery's diverse range of installations.

Storefront is a storied gallery dedicated to subversive architecture and art installations, founded in 1982 by architect Kyong Park in a tiny downtown storefront.

It was later moved into a sliver of a building in the Lower East Side and fitted out with a concrete facade designed by architects Steven Holl and Vito Acconci, with giant concrete panels that swing open and closed.

The institution and its cavernous basement have been updated throughout the years, but GRT Architects' renovation marks the first significant changes to the street-level gallery in twenty years, as well as the first semi-permanent display system for exhibitions.

"Practically, we needed to bring the gallery up to today's standards for mounting exhibitions safely, without having to reinvent the space from scratch every time," Storefront deputy director Guillermo Ruiz told Dezeen.

For the project, GRT Architects created a modular, aluminium shelving system that is affixed to tiny anchors along the gallery's front wall, just far enough away from the facade to avoid collision with a rotating panel.

The system can be completely deconstructed so that the gallery is empty, or various configurations can be slid and bolted into place depending on the needs of an exhibition.

Modular components designed by GRT Architecture can also be arranged within the system at various heights and positions, including panels for projecting video and a shelf concealed by a canvas curtain. The studio primarily worked with customised parts from aluminium framing system company 80/20 for the build.

"It's flexible enough that it's always working well with whatever exhibition they have, " GRT Architects founding partner Tal Schori told Dezeen. "Whether it's video projection or objects or things on the wall."

The studio also added small touches like a mobile desk for a gallery attendant, and a slim, stainless steel handle on one of the gallery's panels that doubles as the main door. Both elements, and the shelving system, were informed by Storefront's industrial, riveted beams.

Read:

SO-IL wraps white plastic around New York's Storefront gallery

"It is a small thing, but it's really significant because for decades Storefront never had a door handle," said Schori. "I think this small gesture is a really nice way to welcome people."

The studio also updated Storefront's small bathroom, covering it completely in bright tile work by Jorge Pardo, a Cuban American artist who sits on the organisation's board.

Other structural updates included reworking the gallery's track lighting and "gutting" its walls, ceiling and plywood floor to minimise "all the weird perturbations, soffits, and bump outs" the space collected over decades of use, said Schori.

The studio also illuminated the concrete letters that spell out an elongated "Storefront for Art & Architecture" sign on the facade.

"It's no longer this dark void on the block where everything else is lit up," said Schori.

GRT Architects is based between Brooklyn and Mexico City and was founded in 2014 by Schori and architect Rustam-Marc Mehta. Schori also serves on the board of Storefront and previously worked at the institution as a gallery manager in 2003, as a first job out of college.

The studio recently completed a maximalist restaurant in Beverly Hills and spoke to Dezeen about the skills needed for adaptive reuse projects.
